posts.title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein.
Introduction
Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen:

If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode.
A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything.
“In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.”
Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual. At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not.
Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize:

High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants.
Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis.

Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail (“Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?”) rises from 0.77 to 0.86, and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~69%). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses.
So, what exactly does factuality mean?
Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1:
Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.”
It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show.
Let’s take another example:
Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.”
Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual.
But what about this?
Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.”
Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis?
Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch.
Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all:
Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.”
Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag.
So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations?
Current Service and Its Limitations
Our current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations:

High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well.
Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction.

Optimizing the Holistic Pipeline
To understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights:
Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls?
Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy:

Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning.
Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps.

This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need.
The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening.
Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model:

Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new information
With confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts?
Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specialized
Instead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about:

Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true?
Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show?

Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors.
Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hid
At this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses?
Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router:
Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model:

Makes an assumption.
Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote).
Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict.

We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which:

Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it.
Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false.

Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality Service
Our findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated.
We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases:

FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check.
PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted.

Results
Based on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines:

Evaluation: Datasets and Metrics
We evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show.
We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below:

Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales.
On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times.
Evaluation Results
The best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold.

Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants.
Our takeaways from this experiment are:

Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts.
Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset.
Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment.
Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline.
Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline.

Alignment with Human Rationale
So far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons?
To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap.

We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator.
Conclusion + Future Work
Overall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service:

On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation.
On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning.

The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be:

Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm.
Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis.

Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

posts.title: Webinar Recap: Agentic Debugging of Embedded Systems With CLion and TRACE32®
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
CLion can now debug embedded targets through TRACE32 and let AI agents start and control debug sessions. JetBrains and Lauterbach presented the integration in a joint webinar, and this post recaps the session.
You can also watch the demo presented at the webinar and browse the slides.
How CLion and TRACE32 work together
Moving from editing source code to investigating behavior on a target usually means switching between tools. The integration brings three capabilities into one workflow:
Develop and debug in a single environment.
Control TRACE32 hardware debugging from CLion.
Give AI agents access to live debugger data to inspect program state and find root causes.




TRACE32 is Lauterbach’s debug and trace toolset. It supports more than 150 CPU architectures and over 15,000 chips, and the same software covers the product lifecycle from virtual targets to real hardware. For hardware debugging, Lauterbach offers the PowerDebug System.




CLion communicates with TRACE32 via the Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP). Lauterbach provides a tool called t32debugadapter that exposes the DAP interface and connects to TRACE32 through its Remote API. TRACE32 then handles the connection to the target, whether it’s real silicon, an emulator, or a simulator.
To use the integration, you need:
CLion 2026.2.4 or later
TRACE32 PowerView 09.2026
TRACE32 Debug Adapter 0.1.2 or later




In CLion, go to Settings | Debugger | Debug Profiles and select the dedicated TRACE32 profile.




There, enter the path to the debug adapter executable, the PRACTICE script paths, and any auxiliary options.
Giving AI agents access to the debugger
JetBrains Air gives you one place to run agents and verify their work in CLion. You can start multiple agent sessions, run them in parallel, follow their progress, and review their changes, whether the agents run locally or in the cloud. Agents get the same IDE context you use, such as symbols, types, and dependencies.
CLion exposes its debugger to agents through the built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which supports SSE, stdio, and Streamable HTTP transports. Because the debugger is connected to TRACE32, an agent can investigate what happens on the actual target. The agent controls the standard CLion debugger, so you can follow the session in the Debug tool window and take over at any point.
Skills tell agents when and how to use these tools. CLion includes a generic debugger skill, clion-debugger, plus skills for hard fault debugging on Arm Cortex-M devices and for RTOS state exploration. 




You can install skills for supported agents from the IDE, configure them manually for other agents, or write custom skills for your project or target hardware. In CLion 2026.2 and later, router mode keeps the debugger tool descriptions out of the agent context until they’re needed, reducing token usage.
The choice of agent is yours. CLion supports agents that use the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), including Junie, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, as well as any compatible internal agent your company builds.




You can use your existing agent subscriptions or API keys. Junie Lite provides a free AI model through JetBrains infrastructure, and the current offer terms are valid through December 31, 2026.
Demo: Debugging a four-core AURIX board
For the demo, we used a 4-core Infineon AURIX™ TC387QP with HighTec TriCore GCC, a CMake project, and a Lauterbach LA-3504 PowerDebug E50 probe. Claude Code converted the project from an AURIX Development Studio project to CMake. The PRACTICE setup and upload scripts were adapted from the TRACE32 examples with minor adjustments. In the demo, the agent starts a debug session via TRACE32 and inspects registers and memory across all four cores. The agent uses the same debugger you do, so you can follow along, pause the session, or take over.






Key Q&A
Licensing
The integration adds no cost on the TRACE32 side. You need the same licenses you would use with PowerView directly. Which licenses those are depends on your target and interface, and you get them from Lauterbach. The skills and MCP tools are included in CLion, which is free for non-commercial use. Commercial use requires a trial or a paid license.
Scope and limits
The integration is at an early stage, and a few things are not available yet:
Instruction and data trace.
A trace viewer in CLion.
Real-time variable updates, which we are adding probe by probe.
T32 commands issued directly from CLion.
For T32 commands, you can use PowerView in the same debug session as a workaround. PowerView does not need to be visible and can run in the background. HSM cores should work whenever TRACE32 can debug them. The debug adapter is an open interface, while the skills are specific to CLion.
Documentation and other questions
In our experience, an agent such as Claude Code parses PDFs well, so you can point it at a folder with target datasheets without extra tooling. Generating a software bill of materials is up to your build system.
Try it yourself
To set up the integration, follow Lauterbach’s article How to Use CLion as Front-End for TRACE32. To try agents in CLion, download the 2026.3 version and learn more in the Air documentation. 
If you want to evaluate CLion for your team, use the CLion trial version or request a demo.

posts.title: Rider 2026.3 for Game Development: Lua and Verse Plugins, Better C++ Debugging, and Closer Godot Integration
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Rider 2026.3 brings improvements to the workflows you rely on to write, run, and debug games. This release connects Rider more closely with the Godot Editor, improves debugging for Unreal Engine and custom C++ engines, adds support for Unity CoreCLR Players, and introduces new Lua and Verse plugins in Beta.
Here’s what’s new for game developers.
Download Rider
                                                    
Lua and Verse: New language plugins in Beta
Lua: Work with scripts alongside your C++ or C# code
If your project combines C++ or C# with Lua scripts, this release will streamline your workflow, as the new JetBrains-maintained Lua plugin lets you work with both in Rider.




The plugin supports Lua 5.1–5.4, LuaJIT, and Luau, with:
Code completion, documentation, parameter information, and inlay hints.
More than 35 inspections with quick-fixes.
Navigation, Find Usages, call hierarchy, and require path resolution.
Refactorings such as Rename, Extract Function, Inline, and Change Signature.
A configurable code formatter.
It also understands existing EmmyLua, LuaLS, and LDoc comments, as well as Luau type annotations, so you can keep the annotations your project already uses.
Search for Lua in Settings | Plugins | Marketplace to install the Beta.
Verse: Native language support
The new Verse Language plugin uses Rider’s own language engine to offer Verse support without requiring an external language server.




It provides syntax highlighting, error detection, code completion, navigation, Find Usages, and Quick Documentation. These capabilities are also available to AI agents through Rider’s MCP server.
For Unreal Engine 6 projects, you can open a .sln or .uproject file to work with C++ and Verse in the same project. For a lighter, Verse-focused setup, open the generated .code-workspace file.
The plugin is available in Beta through JetBrains Marketplace. Cross-language navigation between C++ and Verse is not yet supported.
Command-line argument presets: Keep your launch scenarios ready
With different maps, log levels, and test flags, you often have to run the same game with different arguments.
Rider’s built-in command-line argument presets replace the EzArgs plugin. Create a shared list of arguments, organize them into presets, and choose a preset from the main toolbar before running or debugging.








Presets are independent of run configurations, so you can reuse the same arguments across Debug and Release builds. Arguments support types and validation, and you can toggle individual arguments or entire folders.
Already have a command line saved in EzArgs or elsewhere? Paste it into Import Args from Command Line to split it into arguments and detect their types automatically.
You can share presets through version control or move them between projects using XML import and export.
Godot: Bring your editor, code, and scene together
Debug the scene you’re working on
Rider and the Godot Editor now have a live connection, making it easier to switch between your code and the scene you’re building.
You can debug the current scene in C# or GDScript. If you use C#, the scene launches through the Godot Editor with Rider’s debugger attached from the first frame. You can use Godot’s embedded game window to pause execution or adjust game speed while Rider handles your breakpoints.
You can also right-click a file in either application to open it in the other.
To enable the connection, install and enable the JetBrains Rider Integration add-on from the Godot Asset Store. The connection service itself ships with Rider.
See your scene in the debugger
A variable’s value is only part of the picture when you’re investigating a gameplay bug. You also need to understand where a node sits in the scene and what’s happening around it.
Rider 2026.3 brings Godot-aware debugging to both C# and GDScript. When execution pauses at a breakpoint, you can explore autoloads, the active scene, and its node hierarchy in the live scene tree, then inspect node properties. Nodes display their Godot names and types, making them easier to identify.




GDScript debugging also gains variable inspection on hover, Add to Watches, and code completion for expressions in the Immediate window. Large arrays and dictionaries can be explored page by page.
The scene tree appears when you hit a breakpoint in a Godot debug session. No additional setup is required for that view.
Unity: Debug CoreCLR Players
Trying Unity’s new runtime? Rider 2026.3 supports debugging CoreCLR desktop Players in Unity 6.7. Attach to a Player, set breakpoints, and step through your code using the familiar Rider debugger.
CoreCLR Players are an experimental technical preview in Unity. The Unity 6.7 Editor, including Play mode, still uses Mono. Rider also includes early support for developers testing the CoreCLR-based Editor in Unity 7 Alpha.
There’s more planned for Unity developers: Unity for Agents is coming in Rider 2026.3.1. Stay tuned for a closer look.
Unreal Engine and custom C++ engines: Spend less time getting back to the bug
Update Natvis visualizers without restarting
Natvis visualizers make complex engine types easier to read in the debugger. But adjusting a visualizer has traditionally meant stopping the session, relaunching the game, and reproducing the same state.
With Natvis hot reload, you can edit a loaded .natvis file and reload it during the active debug session. The Variables view updates without restarting the game.




This release also improves expression evaluation and Natvis rendering, including more reliable inspection of Unreal Engine’s TMap and TSet containers, support for additional expressions and visualizer elements, and faster debugger startup for Unreal Engine projects.
Step through C++ code more smoothly
On Windows, Rider now uses a native stepping implementation for C++ code built with MSVC, including Unreal Engine projects. Step Into, Step Over, and Step Instruction are faster and more consistent.
The update also fixes issues that were causing stepping to stop at the wrong locations or leaving internal breakpoints behind, resulting in unexpected stops.
Find what changed a value
When a value changes unexpectedly, a data breakpoint can help you find the code responsible.
You can now set one by right-clicking a variable directly in the editor, or add it through the Breakpoints dialog using a variable name or memory address. Conditions, logging, and read/write access triggers are supported.




AI agents can also set data breakpoints through the Rider MCP server, giving you another way to investigate unexpected memory changes together with your agent.
Try the new LLDB 21 debugger
Rider 2026.3 introduces an experimental debugger built on LLDB 21. It combines the latest upstream LLVM fixes with JetBrains’ debugger enhancements, including MSVC support, Natvis rendering, and Rider’s custom expression evaluator. The experimental debugger is available on Windows, macOS, and Linux.




The default debugger depends on your platform. On Windows, Rider continues to use JetBrains’ customized LLDB 9. On macOS, Rider already ships with upstream LLDB 21, but without JetBrains’ custom enhancements. The new experimental option brings these enhancements to a common LLDB 21 foundation across all three platforms.
You can download and select the experimental build in the Debugger settings. Try it with your projects and share your feedback.
Keep your C++ project structure consistent with Visual Studio
Are you moving from Visual Studio to Rider or working with teammates who use both? Experimental support for .vcxproj.filters keeps your C++ project’s logical structure synchronized between the two IDEs.




For Unreal Engine and other C++ projects, this helps preserve the project organization your team already uses when switching between Rider and Visual Studio.
More improvements for your day-to-day work
Beyond engine-specific updates, Rider 2026.3 brings:
More responsive editing while opening solutions or switching branches, and faster access to highlighting, search, and navigation when reopening a solution.
A Files view for browsing and editing repository files outside your solution, including build scripts, CI configuration, and documentation.
Improved Git worktree support, including the ability to copy local project settings and run configurations into new worktrees.
JetBrains Air, a workspace for running coding agents and reviewing their changes inside the IDE.
Try Rider 2026.3
Update through the Toolbox App or download Rider to try the new game development features.
Rider is free for non-commercial use. To explore its support for your engine and workflow, visit Rider for Game Development.
We’d love to hear how these updates work in your projects. Share your feedback in the comments or report issues in YouTrack.

posts.title: JetBrains IDEs Transformed for the Agentic Era of Development – With Air
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
As agents write more code, individual productivity goes up, but the bottleneck moves to review. 49% of developers now spend four or more hours a week reviewing AI output and correcting prompts (Atlassian State of Developer Experience Report 2026). We believe this means you need to understand what changed, decide whether it belongs in your codebase, and be able to maintain it after the session ends.
This is why we shipped Air in JetBrains IDEs, with the 2026.3 release. This allows you to bring your coding agents into your existing development environment, with one place to track their progress, review their changes, and send feedback. It is a major step in making JetBrains IDEs more agentic, while still respecting classical workflows, where the developer remains in control and at the center of everything.
Air is more than a new place to chat with AI. Because it runs inside the IDE, it brings IDE code intelligence to you and your agents. Through the IDE’s MCP server and built-in skills, agents can check inspections, run your build and run configurations, query your databases, and use the IDE’s own refactorings. In IntelliJ IDEA and CLion, they can also drive the debugger.
Try Air in Your IDE
                                    
In this post: Key features of Air | Coming from AI Assistant | Free AI | FAQ
Key features of Air in JetBrains IDEs
Parallel agent sessions, worktrees, and notifications
Follow sessions across projects in one place to understand which agents are working, which need your input, and which have unread results. Notifications tell you when an agent needs you. Give each agent its own local Git worktree so that parallel sessions don’t collide, and review its changes as with any other session. Worktrees that agents create on their own aren’t tracked in Air yet, but we’re working to make this a reality.
Start sessions from presets
Save the agent, model, and instructions you use for a type of task as a preset. Start a new session from it instead of setting everything up again, and keep separate presets for different use cases.




Your existing agents and subscriptions are supported
Air works with agents such as Junie, Codex, Claude Agent, and GitHub Copilot, and connects to other compatible agents through ACP. Bring compatible agents already installed on your machine or add them from the registry, then choose your model and connect your subscription.
Depending on the setup, that can mean your existing provider subscription, an API key, or JetBrains AI. A paid JetBrains AI subscription is not required.
You can also use your Claude Pro or Max subscription with Claude Code in Air’s terminal surface, which opens as a full-screen IDE tab.




Reviewing agent code and Code Notes
You do not have to write every line to own it, but you do need to understand it. When an agent finishes, open the review panel to see what the session changed, then use the IDE’s own tools to check it: navigate the code, run inspections and tests, or use the debugger. Leave Code Notes on specific lines to request changes or ask questions, and send them back to the session with the code context attached.
Code Notes also work with Air’s terminal agents, so you can review their outputs in the IDE and steer the next iteration without giving up your terminal workflow.




IDE intelligence for you and your agents
Supported agents can use native JetBrains IDE capabilities, including debugging, profiling, database management, and semantic code search. You retain access to the exact same tools to inspect and verify their work.
Code completion and next edit suggestions
Code completion keeps working in the editor as before, and it does not count against your JetBrains AI quota. Next edit suggestions work with Air when you sign in with a JetBrains AI subscription or GitHub sign-in.
Ability to disable Air
As the developer in the driver’s seat, you choose whether to use it, and how much. Ask an agent a question as you work, delegate a change, or keep writing the code yourself.
You can disable Air itself in Settings | Plugins and restart the IDE.
Coming from AI Assistant
Here’s what’s new if you’re coming from AI Assistant.
More usage and quota visibility
Air shows the cost of your current session (in tokens or money) and lets you check your remaining JetBrains AI quota and reset date without leaving the IDE. We’re working on the same view for Codex, Claude, and Copilot subscriptions. Users in organizations get a link to JetBrains Console for analytics or managing their team’s AI use.




Commit message generation
When the changes are ready, Air drafts a commit message from the changes you select. Edit it, then commit when you’re ready.
Air as a tool window on the right
The most requested change was a familiar layout. Air can open as a compact tool window on the right, the layout you know from AI Assistant, or as an editor tab when you need more space. In the bottom left-hand corner of Air, open Settings, then hover over Show Chat and select the In Toolwindow option.




AI Assistant remains available
AI Assistant is still available and supported as a separate plugin until early 2027. If switching to Air hid AI Assistant, to bring it back, press Shift twice, search for “Open AI Assistant”, and follow the prompts. See the guide for more details.
Air comes with free AI
We’ve made our coding agent Junie free to use with its Lite configuration. Sign in with your JetBrains Account, give it a task, and use Air to review the result. It also covers the everyday questions you may have asked in the AI chat. No JetBrains AI subscription is required.
Air in JetBrains IDEs is available from version 2026.3. Update your IDE and open Air. Tell us how it fits into your workflow. Leave a comment below or share your feedback on YouTrack.
Fair use applies. Terms and available models may change.
Frequently asked questions
Can I use my Claude subscription in Air?
Yes, you can. Open the agent menu and select Manage Agents, then for Claude, select Terminal instead of Chat. Start a new session to open Claude Code in a full-screen editor tab, and then log in with your Claude subscription. Claude Agent in Air’s chat view requires a JetBrains AI subscription or an Anthropic API key.
Which coding agents does Air support?
Air supports Codex, Claude Agent (in the chat), Claude Code (in the terminal), Gemini, GitHub Copilot, DeepSeek, OpenCode, Cursor, Pi, Grok, Kimi, Kilo, and many more through ACP.
What is the difference between Air in JetBrains IDEs and Junie?
Air is the workspace inside your JetBrains IDE where you run coding agents and review their work. Junie is JetBrains’ coding agent, which you can use through Air. Air also supports agents from other providers.
Do I need a JetBrains AI subscription to use Air in JetBrains IDEs?
No. A paid JetBrains AI subscription is not required for local agent workflows in Air. Use a supported provider account or API key, or sign in with a JetBrains Account to use Junie Lite for free. Provider charges, usage limits, and fair-use terms still apply.
Does Air automatically start agents or send my code to an AI provider?
No. Air does not automatically start agents or send your code to an AI provider. You choose and authorize an agent before using it. Data handling then depends on the agent and provider you select and their applicable terms.
Where is the AI Assistant chat?
We’ve moved AI Chat over as agent sessions in Air. For quick questions, use Junie with the Lite or Luna model and set Effort to Off. Your previous AI Chat conversations will be automatically converted to Junie sessions, so you can pick up where you left off.
Are code completion and next edit suggestions available in Air?
Yes. Both keep working in the editor. Code completion does not use your JetBrains AI quota, and next edit suggestions are available with a JetBrains AI subscription.
Does Air work with remote development?
Yes. When you connect to a remote backend, Air and your agents run on the backend alongside your code.

posts.title: ReSharper 2026.3: Claude Agent and Codex in Visual Studio, .NET 11 and C# 15 Support, and More
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
ReSharper 2026.2 brought Junie to Visual Studio as ReSharper’s first coding agent. In 2026.3, you can also pick Claude Agent or Codex in the same tool window. All three agents can use ReSharper’s refactoring skill to run refactorings such as Rename. This release also supports .NET 11 and C# 15, and the test runner now supports xUnit v3 4.0 and NUnit 5.0.
Download ReSharper 2026.3
                                                    
Claude Agent and Codex in Visual Studio
Many developers already use Claude Agent or Codex in a terminal or separate app. In ReSharper 2026.3, you can choose Claude Agent, Codex, or Junie in the AI Assistant tool window. Ask your chosen agent to write and edit code, run terminal commands, or explain unfamiliar parts of your solution – all without leaving Visual Studio.




Getting started
Install or update to ReSharper 2026.3, and make sure AI Assistant is selected in the installer. If you don’t see the AI Assistant tool window later, run the installer again and choose Install or Repair next to AI Assistant.
Open the AI Assistant tool window, sign in to your JetBrains Account if asked to do so, and choose Claude Agent or Codex from the agent list.
Send your first prompt. The first time you use Claude Agent or Codex, ReSharper asks for your consent before installing the selected agent, since it’s developed by a third party. If Node.js isn’t installed on your machine, ReSharper installs that too.
ReSharper connects these agents through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), an open protocol for connecting coding agents to editors.
Learn more about agents in ReSharper in our documentation.
Agents can run ReSharper refactorings
Junie, Claude Agent, and Codex can use ReSharper’s refactoring skill to rename symbols or move types to other namespaces instead of editing files one by one.
Junie Lite
Junie Lite, a free model tier for Junie, is now available in ReSharper to anyone signed in with a JetBrains Account, even without a ReSharper license.
Licensing and limits
What do I need to use Claude Agent and Codex in ReSharper? A JetBrains AI subscription. Claude Agent and Codex consume your JetBrains AI quota, as does Junie unless you use the free Junie Lite tier.
Can I use my own Claude or ChatGPT subscription, or my own API key? Not in this release. ReSharper doesn’t use personal Claude or ChatGPT subscriptions, and it doesn’t support bring-your-own-key (BYOK).
Is there a free AI trial? ReSharper no longer offers JetBrains AI Pro trials. If you’ve already started one, you can continue using it until it ends. Junie Lite is currently available as a free tier, with no trial required.
Regional restrictions on the availability of AI features in Mainland China apply.
Day-one support for .NET 11 and C# 15
Microsoft launched .NET 11 today at .NET Conf 2026, and ReSharper 2026.3 already supports it.
C# 15 language support
ReSharper supports C# 15, including union types, closed class hierarchies, collection expression arguments, extension indexers, and labeled break and continue statements. Code analysis, completion, navigation, and other features work with the new syntax. New inspections, quick-fixes, and context actions help you adopt the new syntax in existing code.
ReSharper also supports the memory safety redesign preview. It recognizes the new safe modifier and unsafe expressions, highlights missing or redundant unsafe contexts, and offers quick-fixes for them.




Readable runtime-async code in the decompiler
.NET 11 supports runtime-async methods, which the runtime handles directly instead of through compiler-generated state machines. Runtime-async is still a preview feature in .NET 11. When you decompile one of these methods, ReSharper now shows it as an ordinary async method, and the IL Viewer marks it with the async keyword. The same improvements are available in dotPeek 2026.3.
Code analysis and coding assistance
ReSharper suggests collection expressions in more places, including lists and immutable builders filled with foreach loops, AddRange, or individual Add calls. New inspections catch character values used by mistake as array lengths or indices, flag culture-sensitive operations and implicit string sorting, and find using statements that dispose of a task instead of its result. Another inspection suggests tuple syntax instead of verbose ValueTuple creation.




Parameter information now groups overloads that share the same leading parameters, so long overload lists are easier to scan while you write a call.
For C++, ReSharper 2026.3 adds a class layout view that shows how a class is arranged in memory. This release also brings format string checks for std::format, std::print, {fmt}, and Unreal Engine’s structured logging macros, new refactoring options, and new CUDA inspections. See What’s New in ReSharper C++ 2026.3 for the details.
Unit testing
The test runner works with the latest versions of popular test frameworks:
ReSharper now supports xUnit v3 4.0 and NUnit 5.0.
Test discovery is more reliable for MSTest 4 projects.
ReSharper applies Playwright settings (such as LaunchOptions) from your .runsettings file, so you can run browser tests with the browser window visible.
Microsoft.Testing.Platform support is enabled by default, so ReSharper finds tests for frameworks like TUnit without any setting changes.
Try ReSharper 2026.3
Download ReSharper 2026.3 and try working with Claude Agent or Codex in the AI Assistant tool window. For all the updates in this release, see What’s New in ReSharper 2026.3 and the release notes.
Tell us what you think in the comments below, or find us on X and Bluesky.

posts.title: ReSharper C++ 2026.3: Class Layout, Format String Analysis, And More
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
ReSharper C++ 2026.3 is here, with a new Class Layout tool window that visualizes the memory layout of your classes and helps you spot wasted space..
This release also improves format string analysis to cover std::format, std::print, and the {fmt} library. Other highlights include updates to the Change Signature and Extract Method refactorings, as well as new CUDA inspections.
Download ReSharper C++ 2026.3
                                                    
Class layout
How a class is laid out in memory determines how much space each object takes, how well its data fits into CPU cache lines, and whether it matches a binary format or an ABI shared with other code. To satisfy alignment requirements, the compiler silently inserts padding between fields. As a result, a class can end up noticeably larger than the sum of its members. This can add up quickly for objects allocated in large numbers or processed in tight loops.
The new Class Layout tool window visualizes the memory layout of a class, struct, or union, including the offset and size of every field and bit-field, base class subobjects, virtual table pointers, and the padding between them. This makes it easy to find padding you can eliminate, check the effect of alignas or #pragma pack, and understand the layout of classes in a complex hierarchy. To open the tool window, place the caret on a class name or any reference to a class type, then choose ReSharper | Inspect | Class Layout. Alternatively, select the Class Layout item in the Alt+Enter menu.




Refactorings
Change Signature for constructors
The Change Signature refactoring now works on constructors. You can add, remove, reorder, and change the types of constructor parameters, and ReSharper C++ updates the constructor calls throughout your code, including direct and braced initialization, new expressions, member and base class initializers, and factory functions such as std::make_unique. The Change Signature dialog also has two new options that let you add or remove the static specifier on functions and the explicit specifier on constructors.
Note: Some constructor calls, such as implicit conversions or calls through a custom factory template, can’t be found and therefore aren’t updated.




Extract Method placement
The Extract Method refactoring now has a Place in option that controls where the extracted function is placed: either next to the current function, as a free function in the namespace containing the current class, or as a free function in an anonymous namespace. A new Make constexpr option also lets you mark the extracted function constexpr.




Introduce Using Directive
The new Introduce Using Directive refactoring replaces namespace qualifiers, such as std in std::cout, with a using namespace directive.




Format string analysis
std::format, std::print, and {fmt}
ReSharper C++ has long analyzed calls to printf-like functions. In 2026.3, the same analysis extends to the C++20 <format> and C++23 <print> standard library headers, as well as the popular {fmt} library. ReSharper C++ now analyzes calls to format, format_to, format_to_n, formatted_size, print, and println from both the std and fmt namespaces:
Replacement fields in the format string are highlighted. When the caret is on a replacement field, the corresponding argument is highlighted too, and vice versa.
ReSharper C++ reports invalid replacement fields, missing and unused arguments, and format strings that mix automatic and manual argument indexing.
The format specification is checked against the argument type. For example, formatting a double with the d presentation type is reported, and a quick-fix replaces it with a matching one.
Named arguments are supported for the {fmt} library via fmt::arg.




printf updates
The analysis of printf-like functions now supports the new format specifiers from C23. ReSharper C++ also understands POSIX positional arguments such as %1$s and %2$*1$d, and checks the argument types by position. A new inspection reports printf calls that mix positional and non-positional arguments.




Unreal Engine logging macros
Format string analysis now supports UE_LOGFMT and related Unreal Engine structured logging macros. ReSharper C++ highlights the fields in the format string, matches them with the arguments, and reports missing or unused arguments and invalid field names.




Format attributes on constructors
The [[jetbrains::format]] and [[gnu::format]] attributes can now be applied to constructors, so ReSharper C++ checks the format string in constructor calls. Additionally, ReSharper C++ now recognizes the underscore spelling of the attribute, [[__gnu__::__format__(__printf__, 1, 2)]], as well as constant expressions in the attribute’s argument indices.




Code analysis
Clang-Tidy integration
The bundled Clang-Tidy binary has been updated to LLVM 23, bringing new checks and improvements from the latest LLVM release. Clang-Format has been updated as well.
NOLINT comments with globs in check names, such as // NOLINT(readability-*), now also suppress the ReSharper C++ inspections that correspond to the matching Clang-Tidy checks. Moreover, a new Additional clang-tidy command-line arguments setting on the Clang-Tidy options page lets you pass extra arguments to Clang-Tidy.




Explanations for failed constraints
When a requires expression evaluates to false, ReSharper C++ now shows which requirement fails and why its expression is ill-formed. For example, a function or operator may be inaccessible or deleted, or the number of arguments may not match the candidate functions. Similarly, error messages about deleted constructors and failed destructibility checks now show the full chain of reasons, down to the specific base class or field that causes the problem.




CUDA
ReSharper C++ 2026.3 extends its CUDA support with a new set of inspections, which you can configure in the new CUDA group on the inspection severity settings page:
Execution spaces: ReSharper C++ checks that a function can be called from the CUDA execution space of the calling code, following the rules of the CUDA Programming Guide. The check takes into account __CUDA_ARCH__ guards, CUDA runtime API functions, C library functions available in device code (such as printf and malloc), and calls to overloaded operators.
Memory spaces: New inspections detect invalid uses of the __device__, __constant__, __shared__, __managed__, and __grid_constant__ specifiers. Examples include memory space specifiers on data members or function parameters, initializers on __shared__ variables, and conflicting specifiers.
CUDA Tile: New inspections enforce the restrictions of the CUDA Tile programming model. For example, they report goto and return statements inside loops in __tile_global__ functions, as well as tile kernels launched with a block size other than 1. A suggestion also detects loops that can be replaced with a range-based for over cuda::tiles::irange.




Language support
ReSharper C++ 2026.3 supports more features from recent C++ standards:
C++23 delimited escape sequences: \x{...}, \o{...}, and \u{...} (P2290).
C++26 user-generated static_assert messages (P2741).
C++26 offset parameter of the #embed directive (P3540).
C++26 #line directives before module declarations (P3868).




Visual Studio integration
Out-of-Process mode
In ReSharper 2026.2, Out-of-Process (OOP) mode became the default. It moves heavy analysis work out of the Visual Studio process, helping prevent UI freezes and keep typing smooth. In this release, we continue to polish OOP mode and fix some of the remaining issues:
Includes Analyzer is now available in OOP mode.
Visual Studio’s F8 and Shift+F8 shortcuts navigate between ReSharper’s Find Usages results.
The New from Template command is once again available in the Solution Explorer context menu for C++ projects.
Unit testing in CMake projects
CMake projects opened in Visual Studio’s Open Folder mode are now built before unit tests are run, according to the Build Policy setting of the unit test session.
Tell us your thoughts
This post covered the highlights of improvements in C++ support. Take a look at the What’s New in ReSharper 2026.3 page to learn about all the other changes introduced in this release. Among them, ReSharper 2026.3 brings Claude and Codex into Visual Studio alongside Junie.
Download the latest release and let us know how it works for your projects.

posts.title: The State of Developer Ecosystem 2026: A Decade of Understanding Developers
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
This year marks the tenth edition of the State of Developer Ecosystem report. What started in 2017 as a survey about languages and tools has grown into a comprehensive study of how developers work, what they use, and how the industry is changing.
The 2026 edition is based on responses from 28,945 developers across 198 countries and regions. Here’s what stood out.




AI agents are doing a significant share of the work
The use of AI is now standard practice, not a differentiator. More than half of employed developers use AI agents in over 60% of their work tasks. Despite the high rate of adoption, experimentation hasn’t slowed. Only 23% don’t plan to try any new AI tools in the next year.
How developers work with agents varies with experience. Senior developers go beyond prompts and give agents guidelines, specs, and ways to verify their work. They’re also harder to impress. 60% of developers with 1–2 years of experience say AI-generated solutions are better than their own, compared with 47% of those with 16 or more years of experience.
Token counts don’t tell the whole ROI story
Token usage is the most common way to measure AI’s impact. 51% of tech managers say their organizations track it, but only 30% count it among the most insightful metrics. Net time gain exhibits an inverse dynamic: 39% find it insightful, but only 28% track it.
Satisfaction with AI’s ROI is tied to the company’s size. More than half of tech managers at small organizations are satisfied with the return on their AI spending, compared with 34% at large ones. 40% of managers at organizations that don’t measure ROI say they’re satisfied anyway.
Developers would do it all over again
The job market is tough. Just 18% of developers say conditions in their area are favorable, though Japan is a remarkable outlier, with 43% of developers there reporting favorable conditions. Despite the gloomy outlook, three out of four developers would choose the same career if they could start over. This position was most common among architects, team leads, and DevOps and infrastructure engineers.
A decade of languages
Ten years of data make the long-term trends easy to see. For the first time, Python has overtaken JavaScript as the most widely used language, at 65%. Meanwhile, TypeScript adoption has more than tripled since 2017.




Our Language Promise Index, now in its third year, combines five-year growth, adoption intent, and user loyalty to show how strongly each language is positioned for the year ahead. TypeScript tops the 2026 index, followed by Rust and Python. Rust also leads in the category of highest-paid language skills, alongside Go, and they’re the two languages developers most want to adopt next.




A few more numbers
In database usage, PostgreSQL pulled ahead, gaining nine percentage points to reach 59%, while MySQL held at 54%.
47% of developers program for fun as a hobby.
The pet debate continues: 39% of developers prefer dogs, while 36% prefer cats.
State of Developer Ecosystem 2026 methodology
The survey ran from May to July 2026. After data cleaning, the report is based on 28,945 developers from 198 countries and regions. We improve our methodology every year, and a few things changed this time around:
To filter out fraudulent and dishonest responses, we used 91 criteria this year, almost double last year’s number.
The survey had 535 questions. Respondents only saw the sections relevant to them, and questions were randomized to reduce the load.
We advertised the survey with unbranded creatives. This reduced the bias toward JetBrains users and made the data more representative, but it also means some results may differ from previous years.
We still corrected for remaining JetBrains bias by reducing the share of responses from JetBrains users by 10%.
Responses were weighted by region, employment status, and programming language use, and the survey was available in nine languages. You can find the full methodology on the report page.
Wrapping up
10 years in, the Developer Ecosystem Survey results depict a profession where AI agents are part of everyday work, organizations are still working out how to measure the payoff, and developers would still choose the same career path despite a tough job market.
View the full report 
                                    
As always, the anonymized raw data is free to download on the report page. You can also explore the numbers yourself with the Developer Ecosystem Data Playground. 
Join the conversation
What surprised you most in this year’s findings? Share your thoughts on X or other social media, mentioning @jetbrains and using the hashtag #DevEcosystem26.
Want to contribute to next year’s Developer Ecosystem Survey? Join our JetBrains Tech Insights Lab. As a member, you’ll be invited to take part in the next Developer Ecosystem and other surveys, as well as interviews and UX studies that help improve JetBrains products and provide insights for the developer community. You can also enter prize draws and earn rewards.
See you next year for the 2027 edition!

posts.title: Debugging Rust in 2026
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Rust is a great language for many reasons: safety, performance and tooling. However, debugging is maybe one of the weakest points still. Interestingly enough, the Rust debugging survey 2026 results show that the majority (53.2%) of Rust users don’t use a debugger at all. Many Rust developers (81.3%) say that prints are simply easier/faster. The setup is also another problem: many users find it difficult to set up a debugger and it’s not a beginner-friendly feature. Especially when you include async (28.1%) and macros (23.0%), stepping features break most of the time.
However, the situation is still better than it was in 2021, when the survey was first conducted. The number of users who use a debugger has increased from 36% to 46.8%!
This made me think: how is the debugging experience in Rust today?
So let’s dive into the techniques and tools that are available and how they are used in practice.
The Scenario
We will be using the Graham scan algorithm as an example. The algorithm computes the convex hull of a set of points in a plane: the smallest convex shape that encloses every point. Basically, you can think of it as stretching a rubber band around a collection of nails.
🐀: Here, I built a TUI with Ratatui to visualize the algorithm and the bug:




The source code is available on GitHub.
You can see that it fails to enclose P2: the computed fence is red while the expected fence is green. Now, let’s go through the available debugging techniques to fix it!
1. println!, dbg! or tracing
There is already a unit test that fails, so we can use it as a debugging loop. Simply add println! or dbg! statements to the code and run the test until we find the bug.




Here, we print the intermediate ordering, rerun the failing test and see that points with the same polar angle are ordered farthest-first. Reversing the distance comparison fixes the ordering and the next test run passes.
This is the most common way of debugging in Rust and it works well for small programs. However, you see the problem: it is an iterative and tedious process. You need to recompile and run the program every time which takes time. It is also not ideal for big projects. It still works though!
🐀: What else?
2. rust-gdb or rust-lldb in the terminal
We can inspect the same failing test without changing the source code via rust-lldb or rust-gdb:




From there, we set breakpoints, run only the failing test and inspect the current frame:








At the breakpoint, a is 36 units squared from the pivot while b is only 4. The comparator uses b.cmp(a), so points with the same polar angle are sorted in reverse distance order.
That is the bug: the farther point is processed first and later removed from the hull.
So let’s apply the fix:




We can also use the TUI to visualize it:





🐀: Yay, the rubber band is now wrapped around all the points.
Unlike print debugging, this lets us inspect more state without editing and recompiling the program after every question. The trade-off is a manual workflow: setting useful breakpoints and knowing which debugger commands to run.
🐀: Okay, but is there a more friendly way to debug this?
3. RustRover’s debugger
RustRover is JetBrains’ cross-platform IDE built specifically for Rust. It integrates Cargo projects, tests, code analysis and debugging in one place (and it is free for non-commercial use!).
The recommended way to install it is through the JetBrains Toolbox App, which also handles updates and lets you switch between stable and early-access-preview versions.
RustRover provides a graphical interface for GDB and LLDB, which means we can use the same workflow as before but with a more user-friendly interface. Click the gutter to set a breakpoint, then click the debug icon next to the failing test.




The RustRover debugger documentation covers custom configurations, stepping, watches and expression evaluation in more detail!
🐀: Interesting… I thought this type of debuggers are only available for more mature languages like Python or Java. How does it work under the hood?
Good question! There is actually some interesting Rust-specific machinery behind the debugger. In my Rust in Production episode with Matthias Endler, I explained how RustRover turns the source into its own PSI, then a typed high-level representation and finally MIR. When we evaluate a Rust expression or call a function during a debug session, RustRover lowers it to MIR and sends it to the debugger to execute against the paused process.
🐀: So the debugger actually understands the Rust expression we are asking it to evaluate! Amazing.
Bonus: AI-assisted debugging
Recently we started to see the “AI-assisted” prefix in many things… programming, writing, ordering food, etc. and I thought why not try it for debugging as well?
🐀: So basically ask the agent to fix the bug for us?
Not exactly. The agent is not a replacement for the debugger, but it can help us understand the problem and suggest fixes. Instead, we will ask the agent to debug the problem and watch it in action with RustRover’s debugger!
Starting with RustRover 2026.3, the IDE’s integrated MCP server (Model Context Protocol) can expose the debugger to agents such as Codex and Claude Code. This means that instead of clicking around manually, the agent can start a debug session, set breakpoints, step through the program, read variables and evaluate expressions for us. See what’s new in RustRover 2026.3 for the full release highlights!
Simply open Settings → Tools → MCP Server, enable the server and click Auto-Configure next to your agent. Restart the agent afterwards and you’re set!




Also, see the agentic debugging documentation for more details.
Once the MCP is connected, we can give the agent a goal like this:
“Debug and fix this problem with RustRover MCP “
The result is:





🐀: Oh cool, you’re running Codex inside RustRover with the new Air plugin, and we can watch it run the failing test, set breakpoints, inspect runtime values and fix the bug!
Conclusion
Rust debugging isn’t one workflow. You can use println!, rust-lldb, RustRover or even an AI-assisted debugger. Each has its own trade-offs and is suitable for different scenarios.
🐀: Just pick the tool that works for you!
If you’d like to watch this in action, check out the video version of this post, recorded at Rust Berlin Meetup:






Cheers! 🧀

posts.title: Debug Unity Builds From Rider With the TeamCity CLI and MCP
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
At GameDev Day 2026, TeamCity solutions engineer Artem Rokhin demonstrated how to investigate a CI issue from Rider using the TeamCity CLI and MCP integration.
For the demo, he used a Unity game that worked locally but was missing its background on staging. Though the build had passed, Artem used the CLI to inspect the logs and found an incorrect build parameter. 
After committing his fix, he asked an AI agent connected through MCP to explain the issue and follow the new build.
Let’s go through that example, with the commands and setup you’ll need to try it with your own project.






The problem on staging
In Artem’s demo, a Unity game works locally but is missing its moon landscape on staging, despite a successful TeamCity build. He traces the deployment back to its build and checks the logs and configuration to see where they differ from those in his local setup.
What you need
To apply this workflow to your own project, you need:
A Unity project open in Rider.
A TeamCity pipeline that builds and deploys the project, with its YAML settings stored in the repository.
Access to that pipeline’s build details and logs.
The TeamCity CLI installed on your machine.
For the AI portion, an activated MCP-capable agent in Rider and access to TeamCity’s MCP endpoint. Artem uses Claude Agent.
The recording uses TeamCity Cloud. TeamCity On-Premises users can use 2026.2 as a baseline with generally available Pipelines. See the Pipelines documentation for setup and version details.
The commands below use example IDs. Replace MyGame_BuildWebGL with your WebGL job’s ID, 12345 with the build you are investigating, and 12346 with the new deployment run when you reach that step.
Connect the TeamCity CLI from Rider
Open Rider’s terminal and install the TeamCity CLI if you have not already done so. On macOS with Homebrew:
brew install jetbrains/utils/teamcity
On Windows with WinGet:
winget install JetBrains.TeamCityCLI
Other installation methods are available in the Getting Started guide.
Connect to your server and check the connection:
teamcity auth login --server https://example.teamcity.com
teamcity auth status
Replace the URL with your own TeamCity address. Follow the login flow, which may open your browser for authorization. The authentication documentation covers the available methods.
Once connected, return to Rider’s terminal to inspect the build.
Find the build that produced the game
List recent runs of the WebGL job:
teamcity run list --job MyGame_BuildWebGL --limit 5
Choose the run that produced the version on staging. Include successful runs in your search: In this example, the relevant build is green.
If several runs have completed recently, check the deployment’s source build and revision before investigating. The most recent WebGL build may be newer than the version you have open in the browser.
Inspect the selected run:
teamcity run view 12345
In the recording, Artem starts with the pipeline run, identifies its WebGL job, and then opens that job’s build details. Going directly to the WebGL job’s recent runs is a shorter route when you already know which job produced the game.
Inspect the logs and the configuration
Read the WebGL build log:
teamcity run log 12345
The default log viewer supports search. Press /, enter a term, and use n or N to move between matches. Full command details can be found in the guide to managing runs.
Artem has recently been working with build flavors, so he searches for flavor. The log shows that the build used gameBuildFlavor with the value diagnostic.
That provides a specific setting to investigate. Search the checked-out project for gameBuildFlavor, including both the pipeline configuration and the Unity build code that uses it. 
The value printed in the log tells you what the CI build actually received; the repository helps you trace where it came from and what it controls.
In this demo project, the expected flavor is game. The diagnostic value is associated with the version missing its background. These names are part of the example project’s build setup; your project may use a different parameter or no flavor switch at all.
When you follow a similar lead, check both the definition and the code that consumes the value. Finding an unexpected parameter is useful evidence. Understanding its effect on the build lets you judge whether changing it addresses the symptom.
Commit the configuration change
Artem finds the diagnostic value in the pipeline’s YAML configuration and changes it to game. Because the configuration lives alongside the game code, he can review and commit the change from Rider.
TeamCity is configured to watch the repository, so pushing that commit starts a new pipeline run. You do not need to restart the old build manually in this setup.
For your own pipeline, check its trigger settings and confirm that the new run includes the configuration commit. Keep the original run ID so you can compare the settings and results afterward.
While the new pipeline runs, Artem shows another way to investigate CI results from Rider: an AI agent connected to TeamCity through MCP.
Connect Rider to TeamCity MCP
MCP gives the agent access to TeamCity tools, including tools for retrieving build logs and querying build information. The server endpoint is:
https://example.teamcity.com/app/mcp
For this investigation, create a TeamCity access token limited to the relevant project with the Read-only preset. That is enough to inspect the CI results while you make the configuration change through Git. See TeamCity’s AI integration documentation for token permissions and connection options.
In Rider, go to Settings | Tools | AI Assistant | Model Context Protocol (MCP) and add an HTTP connection. A valid connection configuration should look like this:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "TeamCity": {
      "url": "https://example.teamcity.com/app/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_TEAMCITY_TOKEN"
      }
    }
  }
}
Replace the server address and token placeholder in your private local configuration. Keep the token out of files you commit or share. Apply the configuration and check that Rider can connect. Our AI Assistant MCP guide describes the connection settings.
If you use Claude Agent, also open Settings | Tools | AI Assistant | Agents and enable Pass custom MCP servers. Then select Claude Agent in the AI chat. This exposes the configured connection to the agent, as described in the Claude Agent documentation.
Ask the agent to investigate the symptom
Give the agent the symptom and identify the build. For a similar investigation, you could adapt this prompt:
Use TeamCity MCP to inspect WebGL build BUILD_ID in PROJECT_ID. The game has its background when built locally, but the version deployed to staging is missing it. The CI build is successful. Inspect the build details and logs, then compare relevant settings with the project files. Explain the likely cause and cite the build ID, log entries, and files that support your explanation. Do not change anything yet.
Replace the IDs before sending the prompt. Attach the relevant pipeline YAML and Unity build script if the agent needs help locating them. TeamCity MCP supplies the CI information; the coding agent uses its IDE and file tools to inspect the local project.
In the recording, Claude identifies the diagnostic build flavor and connects it to the unexpected game behavior. It also notices that the correction has already been committed. This part of the demo happens after Artem’s CLI investigation and manual fix, so the response can refer to that existing change.
Check the evidence in the answer. Does it refer to the run you asked about? Does the parameter value match the log? Does the explanation fit the code that consumes it? Those checks make it easier to assess the proposed cause before changing a different pipeline or project.
Follow the new deployment
Artem then asks the agent to check the new pipeline and return the staging URL when deployment finishes. The agent queries TeamCity during the active session and reports progress.
A follow-up prompt could be:
Check the pipeline run for the configuration fix in PROJECT_ID. Report whether the WebGL build and deployment have completed. When deployment succeeds, retrieve the staging URL from the deployment log. If the run is still in progress, report its current state.
For continuous terminal updates, you can also watch the deployment run with the CLI:
teamcity run watch 12346 --logs
Here, 12346 represents the new deployment build’s ID. Use the ID from your own pipeline. Once it completes, inspect its log if you need to retrieve the URL:
teamcity run log 12346
Verify the deployed game
Open the staging URL and repeat the interaction that exposed the problem. In Artem’s demo, the moon landscape is visible again, and the player can drive around it as expected.
This check confirms that the configuration change resolved the observed problem. The earlier run was already green, so another successful pipeline result alone would not establish that the background had returned.
For your own project, also confirm that you are viewing the deployment from the new run. Then compare the result with the local version that behaved correctly.
Make the next investigation easier
The example suggests a few useful improvements to the pipeline:
Log the selected build flavor and other settings that change the game output, so they are easy to find.
Validate the allowed flavors for staging builds in your project’s build script, and ensure that the run fails early when the value is unexpected.
Add a check for the behavior that went wrong here. Depending on the project, that might be a WebGL smoke test that loads the relevant scene or a visual check of the deployed game.
Start with the missing check that would have caught this particular problem. That gives you a concrete way to improve the pipeline, along with a repeatable method for investigating its results in Rider.

posts.title: The State of Go in 2026: What Changed In the Golang Ecosystem Since Last Year
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Every year, the JetBrains Developer Ecosystem survey gives us a snapshot of how developers work. This year, 28,945 developers took part between May and July 2026, and 1,836 of them named Go as one of their primary programming languages.
To celebrate Go’s 17th birthday, in this post, we look at who those Gophers are, which tools they rely on, how AI is changing their day-to-day work, and what the most significant events of this year were for the Go community.
TL;DR:
Go developers are among the most experienced in the survey: 66% have six or more years of professional coding experience, compared with 49% of all respondents.
The standard library has caught up with Gin: net/http is now used by 46% of Go developers for web development, up from 32% last year.
Gophers are heavy AI users, especially in the terminal: 86% use AI coding agents in the CLI at least once a week, compared with 74% of all respondents.
They keep humans in charge: 79% often or always review AI-generated code before accepting it.
The language took one of its biggest steps since generics, with generic methods, encoding/json/v2, and the Green Tea garbage collector arriving this year.
Who are Go developers in 2026?
Backend first, full-stack on the rise
Web services are still Go’s home turf: 80% of Go developers use Go for backend web development, and 49% use it to build CLI utilities and small tools. The biggest shift is in full-stack work, which grew from 30% in 2025 to 40% in 2026 – a trend that matches the rise of TypeScript as Go’s favorite companion language (more on that below).
In relative terms, the fastest-growing task is deploying and managing AI models, which doubled from 3% to 6%. It’s still a niche, but the tooling is maturing. Community projects like Ardan Labs’ Kronk, led by Bill Kennedy, bring hardware-accelerated local inference directly into Go applications.

Happy where they are – with a soft spot for Rust
Most Go developers aren’t looking to move: 70% don’t plan to adopt or migrate to another language in the next 12 months, up from 64% in 2024 and higher than the 63% we see across all respondents of the Developer Ecosystem 2026 survey.
Among those who do plan to learn something new, Rust dominates. Chosen by 16% of Go developers, the share has been holding steady for three years now. We see that they don’t just stop at admiring the language; they actively adopt it – the share of Go developers who used Rust in the last 12 months grew from 14% in 2019 to 25% in 2026, so one in four Gophers now has at least some experience with Rust.
That doesn’t mean Go services are being rewritten, though. Rust is the most desired language across the whole survey, and many developers may be using it for side projects or for narrow, performance-critical components.

Experienced and well paid
Go remains a language of experienced engineers. Two-thirds (66%) of Go developers have six or more years of professional coding experience, compared to an average of 49% of all respondents. At the other end of the scale, only 3% have less than a year of professional experience or none at all, compared with 13% overall.
That seniority is reflected by salary bands as well. 17% of Go developers earn more than USD 120,000 a year, compared with 13% of all respondents, and the share earning more than USD 180,000 is almost twice as high (9% vs. 5%).

Tools and libraries
The standard library catches up with Gin
Go’s standard library has always been one of its strongest selling points, and external frameworks struggle to compete. This year, net/http usage among Go developers rose to 46% (from 32% in 2025), putting it practically level with Gin (48%), which held steady.
Among the other options for web development frameworks, chi (15%), Echo (13%), and Fiber (13%) are the most popular, and only 12% of Go developers don’t use any web framework or router at all.
We can’t measure the reasons directly, but there are a few factors that may contribute to the rising popularity of the standard library’s net/http. Since Go 1.22, the standard ServeMux supports method matching and wildcards in route patterns, which covers much of what developers used to pull in a third-party router for. Meanwhile, the original gorilla/mux, which dominated for a long time but was archived in 2022, is likely slowly being replaced in production projects. Finally, with agentic development on the rise, one of Gin’s primary advantages – handling repetitive tasks – no longer seems relevant, since AI can handle the boilerplate on its own and will favor the standard library to avoid dependency resolution.
Testing frameworks and mock libraries follow a similar stdlib-first pattern: 35% of Go developers don’t use any external frameworks, followed by Testify at 31% and GoMock at 25% – a noticeable rise from 17% in 2024. Interestingly, the share of Go developers who don’t write unit tests dropped to 14% in 2026, from 21% in 2025. This might be because they can now use AI to help with this task; in fact, we see that 84% of Gophers use AI to generate tests weekly or more often – an increase of 20 p.p. compared to 2025!
The starkest contrast is in build systems: 86% of Go developers use go build, while 46% also rely on Makefiles. Other tools (Gradle – 6%, Bazel – 4%) lag far behind.
